headline: Record revenue and fees fuel a strong quarter, dividend up
summary_short: Revenue rose 21% y/y to $6.9 billion and net income climbed 25% to $2.0 billion, with diluted EPS up 25% to $4.81 as fee income grew 20% on record capital-markets activity and PNC raised its quarterly dividend 18% to $2.00 per share.
summary_long: Revenue rose 12% q/q and 21% y/y to $6.9 billion on higher net interest income (+4% q/q to $4.1 billion, on commercial loan growth and FirstBank's first full quarter) and fee income (+10% q/q to $2.3 billion, led by record capital-markets revenue). Noninterest expense rose 9% q/q to $4.1 billion on integration costs and a $140 million foundation contribution; ROTCE was 17.9% and NIM expanded to 2.96%. Provision for credit losses fell to $191 million; net charge-offs held at 0.25% of average loans. CET1 was an estimated 9.9%, down from 10.1%, after PNC returned $1.3 billion to shareholders and raised its dividend 18% to $2.00/share. Q3 buybacks are expected near Q2's pace; no numeric guidance was given.

drivers.explanation: CEO Demchak called it a strong quarter reflecting disciplined execution of PNC's growth strategy, citing the FirstBank conversion, capital position and dividend increase as evidence of the franchise's strength.
Release attributes the increase to growth in both net interest income and fee income, with NII up on commercial loan growth and fee income up on record capital-markets and advisory activity.
EPS growth reflects net income outpacing the 9% q/q rise in noninterest expense, aided by a slight q/q reduction in diluted share count from buybacks.
Tracks diluted EPS growth, driven by the same net income increase against a roughly flat basic share count.
Pretax income growth mirrors revenue growth, as higher net interest and fee income outpaced the rise in noninterest expense and credit provision.
Net income growth reflects revenue growth outpacing expense growth, despite a higher effective tax rate (20.5% vs 19.0% q/q) and integration costs.
Release attributes the q/q increase in common equity to net income, partially offset by dividends, buybacks and a decline in accumulated other comprehensive income.
